company_stages.label: Pre-launch, seed-funded build
company_stages.summary: Rahul Vohra incorporated Superhuman in 2014 after leaving LinkedIn and raised a seed round of roughly $750k–$800k; the amount differs between sources. The first version was desktop/Chrome and Gmail only and took most of 18 months to build. Two to three years in, there were still no customers and few outside users, and the team chose not to launch publicly.

company_stages.label: Invite-only, paid-only, venture-backed growth
company_stages.summary: Superhuman launched invite-only in 2017 with no freemium tier; every user paid $30/month. It raised a $33M Series B in 2019 and a $75M Series C in August 2021. Customer counts stayed in the tens of thousands while the waitlist grew to hundreds of thousands.

company_stages.label: Growth stage moving up-market to teams and enterprise
company_stages.summary: With just over 100 employees, Superhuman shifted from prosumers to teams, enterprise and sales users. It added Outlook and CRM integrations and landed larger enterprise deals, including a 2,500-seat consulting firm deal in mid-2024.

company_stages.label: Acquired; part of the multi-product Superhuman suite (formerly Grammarly)
company_stages.summary: Grammarly announced it would acquire Superhuman in July 2025, and the deal closed in October 2025. Grammarly then renamed itself Superhuman and became a multi-product company spanning Grammarly, Coda/Docs, Mail and Go, sold as a bundled subscription. The combined company reports more than 40M daily users and more than $700M in annual revenue.

strategy_phases.label: Landing-page-led customer discovery
strategy_phases.summary: A landing page collected signups, and each signup got an automated email asking about their email tool and frustrations. This led to hundreds of founder interviews in the first year: about 700 or about 1,000, depending on the source.

strategy_phases.label: Product-market-fit engine before launch
strategy_phases.summary: From April 2017, Superhuman measured product-market fit with the 'very disappointed' survey and segmented to its target personas. It split the roadmap between strengthening what fans loved and closing gaps such as mobile. The launch was held back until the score improved.

strategy_phases.label: Concierge onboarding, waitlist and referral-driven growth
strategy_phases.summary: New users were onboarded one-to-one at a chosen weekly pace instead of through a traditional launch. Referrals let people skip the waitlist. Growth relied on PR, content and organic word of mouth.

strategy_phases.label: Multiplayer features and product-led sales to teams
strategy_phases.summary: Superhuman adapted its existing product for teams. It shipped multiplayer features such as shared snippets and thread sharing, added viral loops on top of them, and ran product-led sales. It also built sales-specific features and integrations.

strategy_phases.label: Suite bundling, acquisitions and AI agents
strategy_phases.summary: After the rebrand, the company bundled its products into a suite, launched Superhuman Go with partner agents, and opened a partner/reseller program. It also acquired or agreed to acquire GPTZero, Fathom and Rows.

tactics.name: 'Very disappointed' PMF survey as the product OKR
tactics.description: Email active users a short survey asking how they would feel if they could no longer use the product. Segment the responses to the most enthusiastic personas. Make the 'very disappointed' percentage the only key result for the product team.
tactics.mechanism: It turns product-market fit into a tracked number. That number guides roadmap choices: what to double down on for fans and what is holding back users who would only be 'somewhat disappointed'.

tactics.name: Human concierge onboarding
tactics.description: Onboard every new user in a live one-to-one call, and fix bugs found in onboarding before the next weekly cohort.
tactics.mechanism: Founder-attributed: onboarded users showed strong retention, low churn, high virality and high NPS, and the calls created superfans who drove word of mouth.

tactics.name: Metered weekly onboarding instead of a public launch
tactics.description: Choose a weekly number of new users to admit from a waitlist rather than opening access all at once.
tactics.mechanism: It keeps onboarding quality high and lets the team fix issues between cohorts. Superhuman founder Rahul Vohra says the purpose was to keep users happy, not to create scarcity.

tactics.name: Skip-the-waitlist referrals
tactics.description: Let existing users refer waitlisted contacts so those contacts get access sooner, using a non-monetary incentive.
tactics.mechanism: Faster access is a strong incentive when demand exceeds supply, so referrals become the fastest path in.

tactics.name: Branded 'Sent via' email footer
tactics.description: Add a product-branded footer to outgoing emails so that every email sent advertises the product.
tactics.mechanism: Each sent email exposes recipients to the brand; this was planned as a virality channel from the start.

tactics.name: Van Westendorp premium pricing
tactics.description: Ask early users at what price the product feels expensive but still worth buying, and set a premium price from the median answer.
tactics.mechanism: It anchors the price to what users will tolerate and supports premium positioning against free incumbents.

tactics.name: Automated founder discovery email to every signup
tactics.description: Auto-send each landing-page signup a short email from Superhuman founder Rahul Vohra asking what they use and what they hate about it.
tactics.mechanism: It turns signups into qualitative research and interview leads at scale.

tactics.name: Open-sourcing an internal framework as evergreen content
tactics.description: Publish the company's internal operating method as a widely shareable article.
tactics.mechanism: Evergreen content keeps driving organic traffic and leads long after it is published.

tactics.name: Non-user collaboration surface with conversion paths
tactics.description: Let non-users view and comment on shared content, using notification emails and paths to sign up.
tactics.mechanism: Collaboration pulls colleagues into the product, creating viral and expansion loops.

tactics.name: Two-stage product-led sales
tactics.description: Staff sales first on 'hand raiser' leads, then use automated outreach for weaker usage signals.
tactics.mechanism: It focuses human sales effort on the highest-intent accounts and covers the long tail with automation.

tactic_occurrences.implementation: Sent the survey via Typeform by email, segmented to founders, managers, executives and business development roles, and built tooling to survey new users continuously.

thirty_second.text: Superhuman began as a paid-only email client and launched invite-only in 2017. Every user paid about $30 a month, and new users were onboarded one-to-one on a live call. Growth came mainly through referrals that let contacts skip the waitlist, a 'Sent via Superhuman' email footer, and evergreen content, all guided by a 'very disappointed' product-market fit survey. It later moved toward teams and enterprise. Grammarly acquired it in 2025 and then renamed itself Superhuman, folding the email app into a multi-product suite as Superhuman Mail.

origin.text: Rahul Vohra founded Rapportive, a Gmail plug-in, and sold it to LinkedIn in 2012. He worked there for about two years, then sketched the concept and incorporated Superhuman in February 2014. He says he conceived it because Gmail and its plugins were getting slower and more cluttered. The idea was a fast, keyboard-driven, offline-capable email client, pitched as 'the fastest email experience ever made.' He raised a seed round of roughly $750K–$800K, mostly from earlier backers, and bought superhuman.com for $175,000, paid over seven years. From the start he planned virality, including email signatures, as a core channel. Design began in January 2015, and the first code was written on May 4, 2015.

first_users.text: A landing page went live around May or June 2015 and drew 10–30 signups a day. Each signup got an automated email from Rahul Vohra asking what email tool they used and what they hated about it. Sources put the number of first-year interviews at about 700 or about 1,000. A Medium post about surviving an acquisition, written after the Mailbox shutdown, reportedly brought more than 5,000 signups. Early targets were founders, VCs, executives and managers at high-growth tech companies. Rahul Vohra personally onboarded the first 100–200 or so customers in long sessions. According to the company, no early user got the product free; even investors paid.

flywheel.text: The early loop appears to have worked like this. Concierge onboarding created committed users, and the company says these users drove word of mouth. Users could refer waitlisted contacts so they skipped the line, and one interview put weekly virally referred new users at 70%. The footer on every sent email reportedly drove 50–60% of web traffic. Later, thread sharing let non-users comment inline and gave them conversion paths into the product. Superhuman reports that launching this feature produced its highest weeks of expansion revenue. It also reports that teams using collaborative features grow seats and revenue twice as fast as other teams.

did_differently.text: Superhuman stands out for withholding a public launch until a measurable product-market fit signal improved, rather than launching early. Rahul Vohra has described resisting team pressure to launch. According to Rahul Vohra, the 'very disappointed' share was made the sole key result of a product OKR. Superhuman also used human onboarding as its go-to-market for a $30-a-month product. It priced at the premium end using a Van Westendorp survey and offered no freemium tier, in contrast to free incumbents.

key_takeaways.text: Segmenting the product-market fit survey changed the picture. Superhuman's score was 22% in summer 2017, and focusing on its target personas raised it to about 32–33%. Product work over three quarters followed, and the score reached 58%. The roadmap was split between deepening what fans liked and fixing gaps such as mobile. Rahul Vohra says the company scaled up once the score was consistently above 40%.

Gating access kept customer counts small relative to demand. The New York Times reported fewer than 15,000 customers in summer 2019, while other sources cite a waitlist of 220,000–275,000 around that time. About 15% of the waitlist used Android and were held back until an Android app existed.

Concierge onboarding was costly to scale. The company has said that in one period onboarding grew from two to six people while support stayed at one person, which led to a backlog and degraded service. It later shifted from 85% concierge to 85% self-service onboarding and phased out personalized onboarding around 2023.

Sharing an internal framework publicly appears to have worked as long-lived marketing. Rahul Vohra's First Round article on the product-market fit engine became that year's most widely shared entrepreneurship piece on the site. He credits this kind of evergreen content with early momentum and ongoing organic leads.

Moving up-market built on the existing product rather than new ones. Superhuman added team purchasing, multiplayer features, CRM integrations and two-stage product-led sales. A year-long consulting firm pilot was followed by a 2,500-seat deal in mid-2024. In October 2023 the CEO said much of the recent growth came from teams.
